quote: Sometimes there’s no beating around the bush. Eloquence be damned: these movies suck.
Your parents told you not to talk to strangers, now film critics are trying to tell you not to watch a trilogy about them either. The stranger danger here is the complete waste of your time.
A particularly savage finale to the trilogy. While it is a little more of what we have seen in the previous films the twist saves it.

Overall, the film seems more concerned with tying up a pre-established structure than with polishing its own internal weaknesses. This sense of "fulfillment" is pervasive on several levels: narrative, formal, and emotional. [Full review in Spanish]
"The Strangers: Chapter 3" is attempting to say something about trauma, manipulation, and the lifecycle of violence — but it’s so underwritten that the themes never really land.

This concluding chapter seems destined to please almost no one other than those mystical, befuddling folks who wanted to know what makes the Strangers tick. And even then... it’s difficult to imagine much satisfaction from such a languid experience.
Most of the creative choices made in the third act range from silly to downright insane as the story really unravels.
What a colossal waste.
Renny Harlin's ill-advised trilogy ends with a whimper.
The Strangers – Chapter 3 brings the story to a close in a fashion that’s more self-assured but still just as hollow, malicious and cumbersome as before. At least the trilogy is consistent.
Beyond disappointing. Not only does Chapter 3 fail to pay off the two previous films, it doesn't even offer rising action or a climax. A colossal disappointment and waste of time
The trilogy concludes with a sense of missed opportunity. It's not a complete disaster, but neither is it a significant evolution of the concept. [Full review in Spanish]

Unless you’re a massive fan of the first two movies - if such a person exists - you can safely avoid this one and hope that, if this property is rebooted again in the future, it sticks to what made it scary and worth doing in the first place.

The finale of this tired franchise only finds a moment of intrigue in the dying gasp of its final seconds, if only because Harlin’s choices are so bonkers it’ll make you momentarily wake up to laugh incredulously.
Renny Harlin’s bloated trilogy concludes on a chapter that shows flickers of life amid the deaths, but there’s no masking the that it’s not nearly enough.
Ultimately The Strangers: Chapter 3 offers no redeemable qualities and is so vacuously unremarkable that it is already in the process of being forgotten.
Don’t be sad that The Strangers franchise is over, be happy……..that it’s FINALLY over.
The Strangers: Chapter 3 fulfills its genre requirements as far as body count and variety of weapons, although it doesn’t have many jump scares.
“Chapter 3″ has its own set of issues. Yet it manages to do a serviceable job tying the trilogy together and bringing it to decent conclusion.
An abysmal final entry in what has become one of the worst horror trilogies in recent memory.

Chapter 3 is a boring excuse of a "film" with zero redeeming qualities, whether intentionally or unintentionally. No, wait, there is one positive thing to say about the film, and it could be the year’s biggest glimmer of hope yet: it’s over.
A long, sad road to create a trilogy that gets to sit on the mantle among the worst film trilogies of all time.
By the end, I wasn’t rooting for the fictional Maya to survive the night as much as for the actress who plays her to move on to better material.

I imagine the creators of 2008’s sleeper hit “The Strangers” never envisioned that nearly two decades later their lean, terrifying premise would be stretched into a trilogy of meandering and creatively bankrupt sequels.
And so ends the most "this could have been an email" movie trilogy in recent memory.
As this so-called "story" tries to wrap itself up, it gets bogged down in exposition and bland philosophizing, offering nothing scary, suspenseful, or the least bit intriguing.
At this point, I'm not even mad. I'm just happy it's finally over.
But here is the twist ending you might not have seen coming: 'The Strangers – Chapter 3' is easily the best of the bunch. It is the destination that finally justifies the journey.
Thankfully, the journey is over for now, and we can become strangers to this failed series, erasing it from our minds

The 2008 original will probably endure as a solid, sleepover-ready example of American ordeal cinema, but this final chapter, like its immediate predecessors, falls somewhere between footnote and outright detritus.
The Strangers Chapter 3 suffers from once again feeling like a piece of a bigger movie, sure. What’s different this time around is that it’s plenty compelling on its own, even in its fragmented form.
It stretches material that wouldn’t overfill 90 minutes to 4.5 hours, arriving at no worthwhile destination and conveying scant excitement en route. It aims low… and still bunts.
This trilogy will be remembered as a bloated misfire.

By the end, whatever squishy goodwill that was left for director Renny Harlin’s three features dries up, leaving only the depressing realization that we’ve wasted four-and-a-half hours of our lives and can’t get that time back.
The movie just never goes for it enough in any direction – whether serious or silly – to make you feel anything.
If Chapter 2 lacked the heart it took to become a cult classic, The Strangers: Chapter 3 is hollowed out completely by its apathetic composition to be anything worth watching.
The theme of what fear can do to a town, almost like a virus, is heavily evident, and our main character Maya, played wonderfully by Madelaine Petshe, is the perfect conduit for it.
It’s largely due to the performance of Petsch that The Strangers: Chapter 3 succeeds at all, by giving us a different look at what it means to be the "Final Girl".
The Strangers: Chapter 3 is certainly the best segment of this frustrating story. But still, the best shit sandwich is still a shit sandwich.
This misfire instead leaves you repeating the original film’s question, "Why are you doing this to us?"
It's finally over.
...all three of these movies could (and should) have been condensed into one potentially above-average thriller.

If "Chapter 2" hid the baggage of reshoots well, here the overbearing feeling that the direction of the trilogy (and its protagonist's journey to the dark side) transformed entirely during production is inescapable.

This film is neither a disaster nor a triumph. It delivers moments of tension and a committed central performance, but stumbles on pacing, predictability, and a curious reluctance to bring its story to a decisive close.
It’s so bad that Bertino should be able to sue for damages to The Strangers’ reputation.
Lacks surprises and suspense while only offering ephemeral thrills and scares. The third time's not the charm.
A stunning bore, wasting whatever potential was there to take the story into a bonkers direction, leaving ticket-buyers with three features of nothingness that should’ve been one terrible movie.
The good news is that CHAPTER 3 is something of an improvement on its predecessors; the bad news is that it isn’t nearly enough of one.
The Strangers: Chapter 3 cements the trilogy’s status as one of the worst ever filmed.

The Strangers: Chapter 3 is proof of what has ruined The Strangers franchise. The last film in this terribly conceived horror reboot trilogy ends with a kill that is so underwhelming and predictable, it confirms all three movies are time-wasting garbage.

The Strangers reboot trilogy comes to a bloody and baffling end in a nonsensical finale that's utterly devoid of scares. An absurd climax literally buries the hatchet in a franchise that never went beyond a tedious exercise in generic horror tropes.
Madelaine Petsch’s stellar performance and facial expressions, and The Strangers: Chapter 3 becomes more than what you would have expected.

[W]hatever the strengths and weaknesses of this movie (and it’s the best of the three, if that’s not damning with faint praise), Basso’s performance [in the climax] and in a church scene with Petsch are enough to tip the scales into the plus column.
They say 'If it ain’t broke don’t fix it,' and they didn’t. They just broke it, seemingly on purpose.
As sketched, thinly, by the returning writers Alan R. Cohen and Alan Freedland, Maya is a shapeless, cookie-cutter final girl -- apropos for this hapless finale, girl.
It’s easy to imagine the nihilistic avenues that Chapter 3 could have gone down.
It just didn't build in the way they wanted it to.
